Mercedes S-Class Recalled Worldwide Over Leaking Front Brake Hoses, 215K Vehicles Affected
89 photos
Photo: Mercedes-Benz
When you're driving a German luxobarge that weighs more than two metric tons, you expect the brakes to work perfectly so, every time, regardless of conditions. Over at Mercedes, the front brake hoses of an estimated 215,231 vehicles may leak brake fluid without any warning.
Per the Federal Motor Transport Authority of Germany, the S-Class recall is referred to as 17121R as opposed to 4391103 in Mercedes lingo. Affected models were produced over five years, from June 2019 all the way to November 2024. The KBA says that 11,828 suspect vehicles were registered in the automaker's home market.
Recall documentation reveals that 223-series luxury sedans equipped with air suspension are being recalled, including Maybach and AMG versions of the Sonderklasse. It should be mentioned that AIRMATIC is completely standard, replacing conventional metal coil springs with compressed air-filled rubber struts.
For model year 2027, suspension options include the cloud-connected Intelligent AIRMATIC setup and the optional E-ACTIVE BODY CONTROL. The former can pre-adjust its damping electronically before reaching any road imperfection due to V2X tech.
Available on higher configurations, E-ACTIVE BODY CONTROL builds on the Intelligent AIRMATIC suspension with 48-volt hydraulic actuators located above the air springs, front stereo cameras that actively read the road, and CURVE mode.
Regarding the latter, CURVE means the massive Sonderklasse can bank into turns like a motorcycle to neutralize lateral forces. CURVE also keeps the body flat under acceleration and braking.
Photo: Mercedes-Benz Given that air suspension covers all versions of the 223 series, that means the Maybach S 680 and the AMG S 63 E PERFORMANCE feature potentially suspect brake hoses. Those hoses carry brake fluid while accommodating wheel movement. Using rubber hoses is a must due to the movement of the wheels, suspension, and steering system.
Leaking hydraulic fluid understandably compromises braking performance, increasing the braking distance. When you're going crazy fast on unrestricted sections of the Autobahn, this kind of leak can end in a big crash because the driver is not accustomed to the reduced braking performance caused by a potential hydraulic fluid leak from said hoses.
Worse still, escaping brake fluid reaches the surface of the road, creating a hazard for vehicles following behind. Transport Canada published a localized safety recall in October 2026, and its guidance warns that brake pedal travel and feel can change dramatically when a leak occurs.
For affected owners, regardless of their country of residence, contacting Mercedes customer service or the nearest dealer is the best course of action. Customers should not interpret the absence of brake fluid on the front hoses and adjacent parts as proof that their vehicles do not fall within this campaign.
Germany's Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt and the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration both identify Continental as the supplier of the suspect hoses. The subject components fail to meet durability specifications when subjected to mechanical and thermal stress, causing the hoses to develop leaks over time.
